summary: An experimental companion to the basic Photuris specification. It defines extensible exchange schemes and attributes, so that future changes can be made without affecting the basic protocol.

eli5.summary: This adds optional extras to the secret-code-agreeing steps, so they can be improved later without changing the main plan.

subtitle: Extensible schemes and attributes for secure key agreement.

tldr.problem: The basic Photuris protocol needs a way to add stronger cryptographic methods in the future without requiring a complete protocol redesign.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines optional exchange schemes, key generation functions, encryption methods, and authentication attributes that can be mixed and matched for different security levels.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can support multiple cryptographic combinations and negotiate the strongest mutually-supported options without changing the core protocol.

today: RFC 2523 remains Experimental and has not been widely deployed. Photuris itself was experimental and did not become a standard; modern protocols like IKE (RFC 7539) have replaced it for key agreement on the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Photuris is a session-key management protocol that lets two parties agree on a secret key over an untrusted network. This RFC extends the basic Photuris protocol (RFC 2522) with additional cryptographic algorithms and methods, all designed to be optional. An implementation does not need to support all of them; instead, the two parties negotiate which methods they both support and choose one that meets their security requirements.

The extensions cover four areas: how to exchange the initial parameters (the exchange-scheme), how to generate encryption keys from that exchange, what encryption methods to use for privacy, and what methods to use for verifying authenticity. Each is independent, so implementations can combine them in different ways.
sections.eli5: Two computers want to secretly agree on a code. Photuris offers many ways to do this. They pick the strongest method they both know, and use that.

sections.title: Exchange-Schemes and Key Generation
sections.content:
An exchange-scheme defines how the two parties create a shared secret from the Diffie-Hellman key exchange. This RFC defines ten optional schemes, each identified by a number (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 20, 28). Each scheme specifies a recommended generator (like 2, 3, or 5), an optional modulus stored in the message, a key generation function (MD5 or SHA1 hash), an encryption method for privacy, and a method to verify the message has not been tampered with.

For example, scheme 8 uses a generator of 2, the SHA1 hash function to generate keys, triple DES encryption (DES-EDE3-CBC) for privacy, and SHA1-IPMAC for verification. The scheme number roughly indicates the cryptographic strength: higher-numbered schemes generally require stronger moduli (at least 112-bits instead of 64-bits).

The RFC also defines SHA1 as a new key-generation function. SHA1 is iterated to generate as many key bytes as needed, taking the most significant bits of each hash iteration and discarding the remainder.
sections.eli5: Each scheme is a recipe that says which math and which cipher to use. Scheme 8 is stronger because it uses triple DES instead of simple DES.

sections.title: Encryption Methods
sections.content:
The RFC defines three privacy methods. The first, DES-CBC over Mask, first masks the message with XOR using key material, then encrypts it with a single DES key. The second, DES-EDE3-CBC over Mask, is triple DES: it XOR-masks the message first, then applies three DES operations (encrypt, decrypt, encrypt) with three different keys, each extracted from separate key-generation iterations. Weak DES keys are discarded and skipped.

The SHA1-IPMAC Check validity method verifies that a message is authentic and unmodified. It hashes a combination of the verification key, the message data, and padding, producing a 160-bit (20-byte) checksum. This is an improvement over the MD5-based method in the base Photuris protocol.

The RIPEMD-160-IPMAC is similar to SHA1-IPMAC but uses the RIPEMD-160 hash function instead, also producing a 160-bit checksum.
sections.eli5: DES-CBC is the basic lock. Triple DES is like three locks in a row, much harder to break. The IPMAC check is a tamper seal that proves nobody changed the message.

sections.title: Authentication Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines six optional attributes that implementations can use with the IP Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). The SHA1-IPMAC attribute (number 6) performs authentication like MD5-IPMAC but using SHA1, which is considered stronger. It can be used for symmetric identification (where both parties share a secret key) or for authenticating IP datagrams.

Similarly, RIPEMD-160-IPMAC (attribute 7) provides authentication using the RIPEMD-160 hash function.

The DES-CBC attribute (8) provides encryption for ESP. The Invert attribute (9) reverses the direction of an encryption operation, allowing the construction of triple DES by chaining three DES-CBC operations with an Invert in the middle. The XOR Whitening attribute (10) applies XOR-based whitening before and after encryption to create the DESX cipher variant, which adds security by mixing in additional key material.
sections.eli5: These are add-ons for the IP security headers. You can pick SHA1, RIPEMD-160, or DES encryption, and combine them to build even stronger ciphers like triple DES or DESX.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using multiple generators and moduli makes it harder for attackers to pre-calculate exchange values for every possible setup. By offering many combinations, the protocol prevents an attacker from wasting effort analyzing a single fixed modulus.

The privacy mask applied before encryption depends on the Security Parameters Index (SPI), which changes for each key agreement. This obscures the number of active sessions between two hosts; an attacker cannot easily count how many secure connections are in use.

However, this obscurement is less effective when the SPI values are predictable or reused. An attacker might still infer information about the number of sessions from differences in the initial encrypted block.

The schemes define minimum cryptographic strength for each combination: 64-bit strength for basic schemes and 112-bit or higher for schemes using SHA1 and triple DES.
sections.eli5: Many choices make it harder for a bad guy to figure out the code. Changing the secret ID for each connection hides how many connections are happening. Stronger ciphers need stronger math behind them.
